args.summary: Female in her early 30s with a continent urinary reservoir (pouch). She had weeks of increasing difficulty catheterizing, so an indwelling pouch catheter was placed. It stopped draining the night before presentation and urine output fell. She then developed severe lower abdominal pain and progressive dyspnea, and arrived in cardiopulmonary decompensation (vitals not reported). WBC 15.3, platelets 513, Hb 143, creatinine 1.08 (eGFR 68), sodium 138. CT with contrast through the pouch: large left laterodorsal reservoir defect with contrast leak into the peritoneum and free intraperitoneal fluid. This is intraperitoneal rupture of the pouch after overdistension, with urinary peritonitis and early sepsis. It needs emergency surgical repair.

args.rationale: Early-30s woman with a continent urinary pouch that ruptured into the abdomen after the pouch catheter stopped draining. CT showed a large left laterodorsal pouch defect with contrast leaking into the abdomen and free fluid. At presentation she had cardiopulmonary decompensation, and her WBC was 15.3 with platelets 513. Emergency laparotomy confirmed the rupture and repaired it; the pouch catheter was secured and a nasogastric tube placed. She was unstable before surgery and is at risk of sepsis from the urine leak, so she needs ICU-level monitoring and support after the operation.
args.followup_or_handoff: ICU handoff: keep the pouch catheter continuously draining. Do not clamp it, and flush it gently as urology directs to prevent mucus blockage. Keep the nasogastric tube on decompression. Continue IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours. Allergy history was not available, so confirm there is no penicillin allergy. Adjust antibiotics once intraoperative or other cultures come back. Monitor hemodynamics, oxygenation, urine output, lactate, electrolytes including chloride and bicarbonate, and creatinine and eGFR (baseline creatinine 1.08, eGFR 68). Watch for recurrent leak or abscess. Urology should follow her daily and plan a contrast study of the pouch (pouchogram) to confirm healing before the catheter comes out. Before discharge, find out why catheterizing became difficult, such as narrowing of the catheterizable channel or pouch stones, and reteach catheterization technique and schedule.
